titre: Nero and the Myth of the Violin During the Fire of Rome (64)
accroche: In 64, it is said that Nero played the violin while watching Rome burn: an instrument that will not exist for another fifteen centuries.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 64, when a fire ravages Rome for six days and six nights, legend has it that Emperor Nero watched the catastrophe while playing the violin. The image is so entrenched that it has given rise to an entire expression, “Nero fiddled while Rome burned,” used to describe anyone who amuses himself while a disaster unfolds before his eyes. The problem is that neither of the scene's two conditions holds up: neither the instrument nor, in large part, Nero's presence at the moment the fire starts.

## What the Ancient Sources Actually Say

Tacitus, who writes under Trajan, some fifty years after the events, places Nero at Antium when the fire breaks out in the shops around the Circus Maximus, on the night of July 18-19. The emperor returns to Rome, he says, only when the flames threaten his own house on the Palatine. On the singing scene, Tacitus is explicit about its status: “rumor had spread everywhere” that Nero, mounting a private stage, had sung the destruction of Troy, comparing present misfortunes with ancient calamities, a rumor, he specifies, not a fact that he puts forward in his own name. Suetonius, later and far more hostile to Nero, goes further and asserts, without that reservation, that the emperor contemplated the fire from the Tower of Maecenas, “exulting,” in his own words, in “the beauty of the flames,” before singing the Sack of Ilium in stage costume. Neither of the two texts, though they are the most detailed that survive, mentions a stringed instrument played with a bow.

## So Where Does the Violin Come From?

The answer is almost comical: the violin, in the form we know, appears in northern Italy in the early 16th century, fifteen hundred years after the fire of Rome. No instrument of this family exists in the 1st century; if he played anything that night, which even Suetonius does not guarantee, it would at best be the cithara, the instrument Nero practiced and for which he competed publicly. The modern expression has thus done two things at once: it has taken as established fact what Tacitus presented as an uncertain rumor, and it has attached to it an instrument that did not yet exist, probably brought in by later translations and popular prints. The Senate, which declared Nero a public enemy after his death and ordered his name erased from monuments, had no reason to nuance his portrait, and posterity, tightening the anecdote as it traveled from language to language, has hardened its features further still. What remains solid, in the two ancient accounts, is something else: Nero reopened the Campus Martius and his own gardens to the homeless, and after the fire had new building regulations put in place (widened streets, limited building heights, mandatory water reserves) that changed Rome more durably than any cithara tune.

carte.punch: Nero did not play the violin while watching Rome burn: the instrument does not exist yet.
carte.idee: The violin appears in northern Italy in the 16th century, fifteen hundred years after the fire of Rome in 64. Tacitus reports only a rumor: Nero is said to have sung in stage costume, not played an instrument, and nothing proves that he saw the fire start.

quiz.question: Why is the expression “Nero played the violin while watching Rome burn” historically impossible?
choix: Because the violin did not yet exist: it is born fifteen centuries later
Because Nero did not know how to play music
Because Nero had left Rome for good before the fire
Because the fire of Rome is a later invention of historians
quiz.explication: Nero practiced the cithara, not the violin, an instrument that appeared in northern Italy in the 16th century; the fire of 64 is quite real and well documented, and Nero survives it by eight years.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Where was Nero when the fire of Rome broke out, according to Tacitus?
choix: On the Tower of Maecenas, watching the fire from the start
On a military campaign in Gaul
Already dead, assassinated a few days before the fire
At Antium, returning only when the fire threatened his own house
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Tacitus places Nero at Antium when the fire breaks out in the shops around the Circus Maximus, and specifies that he returns to Rome only when the flames threaten his house on the Palatine.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What measures does Nero impose on the city after the fire of 64?
choix: He forbids any rebuilding in the destroyed districts
He has the affected districts razed without rebuilding them
He imposes a number of new urban planning rules on the city
He immediately transfers the imperial capital to Antium
quiz_supplementaire.explication: After the fire, Nero reopens his gardens to the homeless and has new building regulations adopted: widened streets, limited building heights, mandatory water reserves.
